author: Jokura et al.
name_in_asr: 砕葉城（スイヤーブ）; 砕葉鎮
asr_identification: Ak-Beshim, Chu valley, 47 km E of Bishkek, N Kyrgyzstan; the inscription found in the Rabat (Shahristan 2)
evidence: Re-study of the Du Huaibao (杜懐宝) inscription: found by chance in 1982 in the Rabat near Bernshtam's excavation point; a dedication for his mother by Du Huaibao, Anxi vice-protector (安西副都護), naming 砕葉鎮 (after Naitō 1997); now in the Kyrgyz-Russian Slavic University museum, Bishkek. New 3D scan and photographs: granite block 32.6 × 13.5 × 11 cm with part of a round pedestal on top, i.e. the base of a Buddha image. Before 1982 Ak-Beshim = Suyab (Clauson 1961) had no strong evidence.
quote: の仮説には有力な証拠がなく確定していなかった…が、1982 年、ラバト内のベルンシュタム発掘地点…付近で、漢文をもつ杜懐宝碑が偶然発見された。…碑文は、安西副都護という役職の杜懐宝という人…中には「砕葉鎮」という文字があり、現在に至るま…で、アク・ベシム遺跡＝スイヤーブ説の確固たる証
note: Agrees with the study (Ak-Beshim = Suyab, high): the inscription naming 砕葉鎮 is the site evidence behind Ji's and the study's identification; the stone is shown to be a Buddha-image pedestal. It is a Tang garrison text (after 679), so it names the Tang fort, not the town of 630 directly; does not change the rating.

author: Jokura et al.
name_in_asr: Suyab; ラバト (Rabat)
asr_identification: the Rabat (Shahristan 2) of Ak-Beshim as the Tang administrative centre of Suiye
evidence: Autumn 2015 excavation and surface collection in the Rabat: the E wall of an inner fortification (SA1501), two rows of grey-green fired bricks and heaps of roof tiles on hardened floors; tiles and bricks clustered in the surface survey; the bricks highly standardised (c. 36 × 16 × 6 cm, mould-made, two complete ones 5.2 kg each), suggesting one production campaign in the garrison period (cf. Wang Fangyi's rebuilding of 679); pottery of the lowest layer (IV) distinct from layers II–III and dated 7th–8th c. The introduction states that the Xiyu ji mentions Suyab as a Sogdian trade city under the Western Turks, and that the Tang garrison and its new wall came later (Jiu Tangshu).
quote: The excavation revealed an eastern wall of inner fortification, greenish-gray burnt bricks arranged in two lines, and several accumulations of roof tiles on hardened surfaces, that might be identified as part of a Chinese administrative center in “Suyab,” a stronghold of the Tang dynasty that dates back to the seventh to eighth centuries AD.
note: Agrees and adds the first stratified Tang evidence from the Rabat (detailed report behind the Yamauchi KAKEN summary): the Tang fort is in Shahristan 2, so the town of 630 is Shahristan 1, as the study already infers. The 7th–8th c. pottery date is typological; no change to the rating.

author: Sims-Williams
name_in_asr: Ambēr (Bactr. αμβηρο); Anbâr, Anbîr
asr_identification: Ambēr = modern Sar-i Pul, N Afghanistan; capital of Guzgan in the 9th–10th c.
evidence: Ambēr = Sar-i Pul 'confirmed' by an Arabic inscription found by A. D. H. Bivar (BSOAS 1966) at the Imām-i Khurd shrine near Sar-i Pul, marking the tomb of Yaḥyā b. Zayd, killed in battle near Ambēr (Yāqūt). Yaʿqūbī (late 9th c.) makes Ambēr the seat of the Arab governors of Guzgan; the Ḥudūd (10th c.) its capital and the market of Balkh. Bactrian loan contract Ss, dated year 476 (= 708 on the era of 233 then assumed), written at Ambēr between 'merchants of Ambēr'; coins of Zhulad Gozgan, 'king of Gar', name Ambēr (mint).
quote: La ville d'Ambër (Anbâr ou Anbîr) est bien connue dans les sources islamiques. Ya'qùbï, écrivant à la fin du IXe siècle, indique qu'elle est le siège des gouverneurs arabes du Guzgan… Ambër a généralement été identifiée avec la ville moderne de Sar-i Pul, une identification confirmée par une inscription arabe découverte par A. D. H. Bivar
note: 01.34: adds an inscription for Ambēr = Sar-i Pul, the basis of Mizutani's 'Anbār?' and of Miyamoto's centre of Gūzgān; but the evidence for Ambēr as capital is 9th–10th c. and its Bactrian attestation 708 (Miyamoto: 698, later era), not 630. 01.33: confirms that the 7th–8th-c. city at Sar-i Pul was Ambēr, which 鋭秣陀 does not transcribe; adds to the case against Sar-i-pul there.

author: Sims-Williams
name_in_asr: Guzgan/Juzjan; Gurziwân; Kundarm; Gaz/Lizg; Dar-i Andara
asr_identification: royal residences of Guzgan in the mountains S/SE of Maymana (Gurziwān, Kundarm), and the fortress Gaz 'in the district of Andar', either near Dar-i Andara (9 km from Maymana) or further E at Darra Gaz/Jazzah S of Balkh
evidence: Seven or eight Bactrian legal documents from Guzgan (two said to come from the Mazar-i Sharif area), dated 648–732, name the rulers Kanag Gozgan (648), Skag Gozgan (684), Yan Gozagan 'king of Gar' (732) and places of Guzgan; the 648 sale contract refers to the 'khaghan's tax' (Western Turkic overlordship). Doc. S (702) was written 'at Gaz, at Wanindan, in the court of the fortress', suggesting the ruler sometimes held court at Gaz; R 'at Gaz, in the district of Andar'. Ḥudūd: the old residence of the Guzgan kings was at Gurziwān; Yaʿqūbī: they lived at 'Kundarm and Kurzumān', in the mountains SE of Maymana, Kundarm further E towards Ambēr. Kalf (doc. O) = Kālif/Kelif on the Oxus, Guzgan's northern limit.
quote: l'ancienne résidence des rois du Guzgan était à Gurziwân ; Ya'qûbï indique qu'ils vivaient habituellement à « Kundarm et Kurzumàn », qu'il traite comme formant une seule et même ville18. Gurziwân, dont Kurzumân est considéré comme une simple variante, se trouve dans les montagnes au sud-est de Maymana.
note: Bears on the capital of 01.34, which the study leaves open with Sar-i Pul as 'perhaps': the pre-Islamic kings resided in the mountains (Gurziwān/Kundarm) and held court at the fortress Gaz, while Ambēr appears as the Arab governors' seat and a market town. So the seat in Xuanzang's time may have been a mountain residence rather than Ambēr; alternatives recorded, capital stays open. District unaffected (documents of 648 already call the country Gozgan).

author: Sims-Williams
name_in_asr: Jiezhi 揭職; Darra Gaz; Gaz
asr_identification: 揭職 = Bactrian γαρσιγο (Gharchistan), after Yoshida 1998; not Darra Gaz
evidence: Note 21: the identification of Darra Gaz (a village 30 miles S of Balkh) with 揭職 (Beal) or with the Tang 奇沙 is 'phonologically impossible': 揭職 EMC kiat-tɕik, Pelliot *Karcik/*Kacik; Yoshida convincingly identifies 揭職 with Bactrian γαρσιγο(στανο) 'Gharchistan'.
quote: ou avec Jiezhi $H§!5, région visitée par Xuanzang dans les années 630 à environ 100 // au sud de Balkh (Beal, loc. cit.), mais l'une et l'autre propositions paraissent impossible phonologiquement.
note: Already used in the 01.36 note (Name paragraph): agrees with the study (*Garčig, 'mountain land'; Darrah Gaz only as an approximate halt). Nothing new to fold.

author: Ogihara and Ching
name_in_asr: Yurpāṣka Monastery
asr_identification: the Kizil grottoes, Kucha region
evidence: Edition of Kuchean (Tocharian B) wooden tablets in St Petersburg (SI 3656 etc.) tied to the Yurpāṣka monastery, located at the Kizil grottoes; SI 1931 records three currencies, which the authors say supports Xuanzang's description of Kucha's gold, silver and copper coins.
note: Not a Xiyu ji place: Yurpāṣka (Kizil) is not one of the monasteries Xuanzang names, and the currency remark is about content, not location. Counted as read.

author: Xinjiang Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology (Wang Yongqiang)
name_in_asr: 龟兹故城; 都护府城
asr_identification: the Kucha old city (龟兹故城, Pilang) under modern Kuqa, Aksu prefecture, Xinjiang: walled city whose E wall adjoins the Youyilu cemetery
evidence: 2025 excavation (July–Dec) at the Youyilu cemetery, NW of the Youyi Lu / Wenhua Lu crossing, E of the E wall of the Kucha old city: 510 tombs (Warring States, Wei-Jin and Tang), a section of the city's E wall (rammed earth, 8.5 m wide, 1.98 m high as preserved) and of its moat (c. 3 m deep, 8 m wide). Tang brick tomb M138 (the only one in southern Xinjiang) with an epitaph of 尹公, 'late Tang commissioner of the Four Garrisons', naming the post 安西副都护 and recording burial 'on the Wulei plain east of the Protectorate city' (都护府城东乌垒原). The wall itself is not dated in the summary.
quote: 龟兹故城东墙东侧。…发掘区域西北部清理出龟兹故城东城墙一段与护…城河遗存，其中城墙由夯土垒筑而成，残宽 8.5 米，残高 1.98…“以四月十四日进厝于都护府城…东乌垒原□□也”
note: Agrees with Ji (capital probably the Pilang old city) and the study (Kucha). Adds site evidence for the Tang city: an epitaph places the tomb east of the Anxi Protectorate city, and the cemetery lies against the E wall of the walled old city, so the old city under Kuqa is the Tang protectorate seat at Kucha. The wall's 7th-c. date and the identity of this city with the capital of 630 are inferred, not shown. A project summary, no plan or section published here.

author: Xubbalieva
name_in_asr: Suye; Mingbulak; Issyk-Kul; Muzart
evidence: Short survey comparing the Xiyu ji with the Xin Tangshu for the Tianshan route (Bālukā, Muzart pass, Issyk-kul, Suye, Mingbulak, Talas, Tashkent); cites A. Khodjayev for Suye at 'Tarozga' = Tokmok; converts li at fixed rates (1 li = 0.576 km); no fieldwork or new evidence.
note: Repeats standard identifications (Issyk-kul, Suyab near Tokmak, Mingbulak) without new evidence and with confused details; adds nothing. Counted as read.

author: Kubaev and Yusupova
name_in_asr: Kanka; Shi-Zheshi; Harashket
asr_identification: Kanka ruins, Akkurgan district, Tashkent region, Uzbekistan, 70 km SW of Tashkent on the old Akhangaran channel
evidence: Reports that Kanka (occupied end of the 4th c. BC to the 12th c. AD) is identified with Antioch on the Jaxartes, Yueni and 'Shi-Zheshi' of the Chinese sources (Bichurin) and Kharashkat of the medieval sources (Masson 1934). 2021 excavation E of the citadel in Shahristan 1: the city temple of the 3rd–6th c. (a fire-temple precinct), levelled in the 8th c. and replaced by a N–S hall of the late 8th–early 9th c. (perhaps a mosque after the Arab conquest of Chach, 739).
quote: The city existed from the end of the 4th century BC to the 12th century AD and is identified by researchers with Antioch of Yaksart (in ancient sources), Yueni, Shi-Zheshi (in Chinese sources) and Harashket (in medieval sources) (Bichurin, 1950: 186-187).
note: Background for 01.09 (study: Tashkent, district on the name): Kanka is a candidate for the chief town of Chach in the early medieval period, alongside Ji's Binkath and the Tashkent sites; it does not discuss Xuanzang or a 7th-c. capital. No change.

author: Mukhamedov
name_in_asr: Choch (Chach); Qanga; Mingorik; Jabgukat
asr_identification: capital of Chach in the 7th–8th c.: Kanka (Akkurgan district) earlier and/or Mingurik (in Tashkent) later; Jabgukat (Aq-ota ruin near Dormon, NE of Tashkent) the yabghu's camp
evidence: Summary of earlier views (Buryakov and others) on the centres of the Turkic rulers of Chach in the 7th–8th c.: (1) Kanka and Mingurik both capitals, Kanka earlier, Mingurik later; (2) Kanka the capital, Mingurik a fortress; (3) Kanka the seat of the Chach tegins, Mingurik, Tarband and Tunkat seats of the tuduns. Jabgukat, 2 farsakhs from Binkat on the Chirchik (Iṣṭakhrī, Ḥudūd), placed at the Aq-ota ruin NE of Tashkent (18 ha).
quote: It is possible that the ruins of the city of Qanga in the Akkurgan district and the ruins of the city of Mingorik in the city of Tashkent were also the capital of Choch. Perhaps earlier, Qanga, and later Mingorik served as the capital.
note: Reports, without new evidence, that the 7th-c. capital of Chach is disputed between Kanka (70 km SW of Tashkent) and Mingurik (in Tashkent); Ji has Binkath. The study's point (Tashkent) is a district-level placement and stands; the capital Xuanzang saw is open among these. Journal of uncertain standard.

author: Matbabayev et al.
name_in_asr: Ershi; Davan
asr_identification: Mingtepa, Andijan region, Uzbekistan = Ershi, capital of Han-period Dayuan
evidence: Summary of the Uzbek-Chinese excavations at Mingtepa (4th c. BC – 4th c. AD): walls, gates, towers, cemetery; argues Mingtepa = Ershi (貳師), capital of Dayuan.
note: Pre-dates Xuanzang by centuries; 01.10 is hearsay and the Xiyu ji names no capital of Ferghana. Adds nothing to the study. Counted as read.

author: Galambos
evidence: How the Ōtani expeditions and Stein invoked Xuanzang (Taizong's preface, Pure Land framing; Stein with Abbot Wang); historiography, no site identification.
note: No location of any Xiyu ji place is argued or tested. Counted as read.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 阿耆尼; ”u shi ri’i yul; gloss ”ak sū
asr_identification: gloss: Aksu (wrong; Takata: Agni is at Karashahr)
evidence: Gloss 'deng sang ”ak sū zer' (now called Aksu) to 阿耆尼 (3b5); Takata: Agni is at Karashahr, far from Aksu; the glossator was probably misled by Gombojab's rendering ”u shi ri, which suggests Uch (Turfan) near Aksu.
quote: 從其所記音推斷，當是阿克蘇。但實際上，阿耆尼位於今哈喇沙爾（Karashahr），與阿克蘇未免相距甚遠。
note: Differs from the study (Karashahr oasis) but is an error explained by the translation's spelling; no weight. Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 屈支; gu tshe’ zhes bya ba’i yul; gloss khu ṭe
asr_identification: gloss: Kucha (庫車), correct
evidence: Gloss 'dang sang khu ṭe zer' (now called Kuche) to 屈支 (4a5); Takata: correct both geographically and phonetically.
quote: 將「屈支」注為「khu ṭe（庫車）」，從地理和記音兩方面來說均無問題。
note: Agrees with the study (Kucha); adds nothing beyond the name continuity. Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 跋禄迦; bha ro ka’i yul; gloss tu shu ta [ ] [ ]
asr_identification: gloss unidentified; Takata lists the capital candidates Aksu, Baicheng, Yakaariq, Kara-yulgun
evidence: Gloss 'deng sang tu shu ta [ ] [ ] zer' to 跋禄迦 (6a1), partly illegible; Takata finds no place name of that sound along the Tianshan foot, and lists the current views of the capital: Aksu, Baicheng, Yakaariq, Kara-yulgun.
quote: 關於跋禄迦國都城的位置，今日有諸說，如阿克蘇、拜城、雅卡阿里克、喀拉玉爾滾等。其位置肯定是在天山山麓某處
note: No identification; Takata's list of candidates matches the study's (capital undecided). Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 大清池 (熱海, 鹹海); mtsho dangs mo che; gloss to si khe la
asr_identification: gloss: Tuz-köl, the Kyrgyz name of Issyk-kul; correct
evidence: Gloss 'deng sang to si khe la zer' to 大清池 (6b1) = Kyrgyz туз көл 'salt lake', a local name of Issyk-kul, also in the Xiyu tongwen zhi (圖斯庫勒, Burut = Kyrgyz 'salt'). Takata takes 大清池 as Issyk-kul.
quote: 此處的「大清池」，即今伊塞克湖（Issyk kul）。「今地名」注為「to si khe la」，即伊塞庫勒（ысык кѳл），現在當地住民吉爾吉斯人稱此地為「方圖斯庫勒（туз кѳл）」
note: Agrees with the study (Issyk-kul); a correct gloss, and it matches the Xiyu ji's own note 又謂鹹海 (salt sea). Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 千泉; chu mig stong; gloss he sa ken
asr_identification: gloss 'he sa ken', perhaps 'land of the Kazakhs'; no place
evidence: Gloss 'deng sang he sa ken zer' to 千泉 (7a3), hard to understand; Takata suggests 'Kazakh' + -kent 'town, land'. He places 千泉 on the N foot of the Kirgiz range, W of Suyab (= Ak-Beshim, proved by the Du Huaibao stele).
quote: 所指無疑是吉爾吉斯山脈北麓水草豐茂的土地。此地今為吉爾吉斯坦與哈薩克斯坦接壤處，所謂「he sa ken」或為哈薩克之音寫亦未可知。
note: No site; a vague regional label. Takata's own placing agrees with the study (Merke area, N foot of the Kirgiz range). Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 葉河; chu klung ’dab ma can; gloss ta la’ si
asr_identification: gloss: Taraz (Talas), wrong; Takata: the Syr Darya
evidence: Gloss 'deng sang ta la’ si zer' at 東臨葉河 (8a4) = Taraz; Takata: the 葉河 is the Syr Darya, the border river between Chāch (Tashkent) and Sutrūṣṇa; Taraz lies over 300 km from it, and Xuanzang's 呾邏私 is a different place W of 千泉.
quote: 「ta la’ si」無疑即是指今哈薩克斯坦的塔拉茲城…實際上塔拉茲城與葉河的直線距離超過300公里
note: Differs from the study (Syr Darya) by an obvious error; Takata agrees with the study. No weight. Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 波吒釐子城; paṭa li puṭa; gloss paṭṇa
asr_identification: gloss: Patna, correct
evidence: Gloss 'deng sang paṭṇa zer' (now called Patna) to the old city S of the Ganges (89a1), with a second gloss restoring the Sanskrit paṭa li puṭa against Gombojab's 'bu' (putra translated).
quote: 而現代印度將Pāṭaliputra稱為「巴特那（Paṭnā）」這一點，也頗為耐人尋味。
note: Agrees with the study (Patna); an 18th-c. Tibetan witness to the identification, no evidential weight. Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 矩奢揭羅補羅城 (上茅宮城); ku sha’i grong khyer; gloss brga rdha
asr_identification: gloss 'brga rdha', unidentified (Takata: Rājagṛha = Rajgir)
evidence: Gloss 'dang sang brga rdha zer' to 矩奢揭羅補羅 (105b1); Takata cannot identify it.
quote: 此處今地名注為「brga rdha」，此處用了極具藏文風格的前加字及上加字，具體所指為何，目前尚無頭緒。
note: No identification; adds nothing. Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 安呾羅縛國; ”a nta ra ba’i yul; gloss be lu ra
asr_identification: gloss 'be lu ra', perhaps Balti (Baltistan), wrong; Takata: Andarāb, S Baghlan province
evidence: Gloss 'dang sang be lu ra zer' to 安呾羅縛國 (143a3); Takata places the country on the Doshi river in S Baghlan, Afghanistan, finds no matching name there, and guesses Balti (巴勒提 of the Qing Xiyu tuzhi), far away; a sign of the glossator's poor knowledge.
quote: 因此為何將「安呾羅縛國」注為「be lu ra」，頗令人費解。筆者認為，或許「be lu ra」是指「巴勒提」（Balti）。
note: Differs from the study (Andarāb) by error; Takata agrees with the study. No weight. Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 烏鎩國; ”u sha’i yul; gloss ’o zhi
asr_identification: gloss: Uch(-Turfan) near Aksu, wrong; Takata: current views Yangi Hissar or Yarkand
evidence: Gloss 'dang sang ’o zhi zer' to 烏鎩國 (147b2) = 烏什 Uch (Xiyu tongwen zhi ”u zhi), c. 80 km NW of Aksu, far from both current candidates, Yangi Hissar and Yarkand; prompted by the sound ”u sha.
quote: 烏鎩國的位置現無定說，比較有影響力的兩種學說是英吉沙（Yanggi-Hissar）說及莎車（Yarkhand）說。…這一條注文也是錯誤的。
note: Differs from both of the study's open alternatives by error; Takata reports the same two alternatives the study holds open. No weight. Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 佉沙國; kha sha’i yul; ka si kā ra
asr_identification: gloss: Kashgar, correct
evidence: Note 'ka si kā ra' to 佉沙國 (148b2), without the deng sang formula; Takata: correct, influenced by Qing 喀什噶爾 (Xiyu tongwen zhi kha shi kar).
quote: 佉沙國作「ka si kā ra」，無誤。
note: Agrees with the study (Kashgar). Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.

author: Takata
name_in_asr: 斫句迦國; sho gu ka’i yul; gloss yer khen
asr_identification: gloss: Yarkand; Takata: the usual identification is Karghalik (Yecheng), a different town
evidence: Gloss 'deng sang yer khen zer ba de yin' to 斫句迦國 (148b6) = Yarkand (莎車); Takata: 斫句迦 is generally taken for Qing Karghalik (Yecheng), and Yecheng and Yarkand are two different towns.
quote: 斫句迦國一般被認為是清代的哈爾噶里克（Karghalik），即今葉城。「今地名」注作「yer khen」，即葉爾羌（Yarkhand，今莎車）。
note: Differs from the study (Karghalik) by placing it at the neighbouring Yarkand; an imprecise gloss, no weight. Value: an anonymous interlinear 'present name' (deng sang … zer) in the Ōtani manuscript of Gombojab's Tibetan translation (made from the Qianlong 'Dragon' Tripiṭaka text, before c. 1747), the glosses added in the later 18th c. after the Dzungar conquest; Takata finds most of them wrong and of little use for historical geography.
